options.content: An organisation that helps new start-ups with workspace, mentoring and training
options.rationale: Correct: it nurtures young businesses.

options.content: A factory that mass-produces electronic components
options.rationale: That is a manufacturer.

options.content: A government office that registers new companies and collects their taxes
options.rationale: That is a revenue authority.

options.content: A bank that only lends to large companies
options.rationale: Incubators support small start-ups.

explanation: Incubators support early-stage start-ups with cheap space, mentoring, training and links to investors.

stem: What is the **first** stage of design thinking?

options.rationale: Correct: understand the users and their needs first.
Prototyping comes after ideas are generated.
Testing is the last stage.
Ideas come after the problem is defined.

explanation: The stages are Empathise, Define, Ideate, Prototype, Test.

stem: Which statement best describes a **science park**?

options.content: A site near a university where technology firms are located together
options.rationale: Correct: firms share facilities and work with researchers.

options.content: A public park with free Wi-Fi for students
options.rationale: This is not a business site.

options.content: A short holiday course that teaches coding skills to school learners
options.rationale: That is a training course.

options.content: A shop that sells scientific equipment
options.rationale: That is a retailer.

explanation: A science park houses technology and research-based firms close to a university or research centre.

stem: How do **academic institutions** mainly support technopreneurship?

options.content: By collecting taxes from new businesses
options.rationale: That is a government role.

options.content: By training skilled graduates and doing research that can become products
options.rationale: Correct: they supply human capital and new knowledge.

options.content: By selling finished products directly to customers in local markets
options.rationale: Universities do not usually sell products.
That is the role of a regulator.

explanation: Universities and colleges educate skilled people and carry out research, and many run innovation hubs.

stem: A mobile banking app adds a feature that lets users download their statement as a PDF. What type of innovation is this?

options.rationale: Radical innovation is a completely new technology.
It does not replace an established market.
Correct: a small improvement to an existing product.
It is being used, so it is an innovation.

explanation: Small improvements to an existing product are incremental innovation.

stem: What is the difference between an **invention** and an **innovation**?

options.content: An invention always makes more money than an innovation, because it is completely new
options.rationale: Many inventions never make money.

options.content: An innovation is an idea that has been turned into something people use
options.rationale: Correct: innovation creates value from ideas.

options.content: An innovation must always be a physical device
options.rationale: Services and processes can be innovations.

options.content: They mean exactly the same thing in business
options.rationale: They are different.

explanation: An invention is a new idea or device; it becomes an innovation when it is put into use and creates value.
hints: Is the idea being used and creating value?

stem: A team draws paper sketches of an app's screens and asks farmers to try them. Which design thinking stages are these?

options.rationale: These come earlier, understanding users and stating the problem.
Ideas are not yet being tried by users here.
Correct: building a quick model, then trying it with users.
No brainstorming or interviewing is described.

explanation: Making paper screens is prototyping; asking farmers to try them is testing.
hints: Which stage builds quick, cheap versions?

stem: Two school leavers in Gweru have a prototype app but no business experience, no office and no investors. Which part of the ecosystem would help them **most** now?

options.rationale: Science parks suit established, growing firms.
Sales help is premature without a business.
Correct: mentoring, cheap space and investor links suit an early start-up.
They need support, not tax collection.

explanation: Incubators exist for exactly this stage: early start-ups needing space, mentoring and contacts.
hints: Which support does a brand-new, two-person start-up need most?

stem: Design thinking starts by understanding the needs of the people who have the problem.
explanation: True. The first stage, empathise, focuses on users before any solution is considered.

stem: Design thinking is always completed in one pass, with no going back to earlier stages.
explanation: False. It is iterative: test results often send the team back to define, ideate or prototype again.

stem: Match each component of the ecosystem to how it supports technopreneurs.

right.content: Creates and tests new technologies and prototypes
Trains skilled graduates and runs innovation competitions
Mentoring and cheap workspace for new start-ups
Premises for growing technology firms near researchers

explanation: Incubators nurture; science parks house; R&D centres create and test; academic institutions educate.

stem: A team designs a water-saving system for a school. Match each activity to its design thinking stage.

left.content: Interviewing the groundsman about watering the gardens
Writing: 'The school needs to water gardens using less borehole water'
Listing twenty possible ideas on a board
Building a cardboard model of a drip system

explanation: Interviewing: empathise. Problem statement: define. Brainstorming: ideate. Model: prototype.

stem: Complete the stages of design thinking in order.
hints: Five stages, starting with understanding users.

stem: What does the abbreviation **R&D** stand for?
Describe **four** ways an incubation centre supports a new technology start-up.

points.description: Low-cost workspace with internet and power
Mentoring / advice from experienced business people
Training in business skills (business plans, marketing, finance)
Networking and introductions to investors / help with registration and legal issues / shared equipment

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: It gives the start-up a cheap desk with reliable internet and power, assigns a mentor who has run a business, runs workshops on writing a business plan, and introduces the founders to investors at pitch events.

explanation: Incubators provide space, mentoring, training and contacts.

stem: Apply the five stages of design thinking to this problem: patients at a rural clinic wait many hours because they do not know when the nurse will be free.

points.description: Empathise: interview/observe patients and nurses to understand the waiting
Define: a clear problem statement from the patients' point of view
Ideate: several possible solutions (e.g. SMS queue numbers, booking by phone, a display board)
Prototype: a quick, cheap version of the chosen idea (e.g. paper tickets with SMS)
Test: patients try it, feedback is collected and the idea improved / repeat

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Empathise: watch the queue and talk to patients and nurses. Define: 'Patients need to know when they will be seen so they can wait elsewhere.' Ideate: SMS queue numbers, phone bookings, a number display. Prototype: hand out numbered tickets and send a text when a patient is three places away. Test: try it for a week, ask for feedback and improve it.

explanation: Each stage should be applied to the clinic problem.
hints: One sentence per stage, all about the same problem.

stem: Tatenda has invented a low-cost solar charger for phones while studying at a polytechnic in Harare. He wants to turn it into a business.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Tatenda has a working prototype but no company and no business skills. Where should he go first?

options.rationale: For growing firms.
Far too early.
He has no product ready for shops.
Correct.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Match each type of support to the part of the ecosystem that provides it.

left.content: Testing the charger's battery life in a laboratory
Lectures in electronics that gave Tatenda his skills
A unit beside other energy firms once the company grows

parts.explanation: Lab testing: R&D centre. Lectures: academic institution. Premises for growing firm: science park.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain whether Tatenda's charger is an invention, an innovation, or both.

points.description: It is an invention (a new device he created)
It becomes an innovation when it is produced and used by customers / creates value

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The charger is an invention because it is a new device. It becomes an innovation once it is made and sold and people use it to charge their phones.

explanation: (a) Incubation centre. (b) R&D centre, academic institution, science park.

stem: A company built an expensive farming app without speaking to any farmers. Few farmers downloaded it.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Which design thinking stage did the company skip?

options.rationale: It built a full app, beyond a prototype.
It had an idea.
Not a design thinking stage.
Correct: it never learnt the farmers' needs.

parts.explanation: Without empathising, the company did not understand its users.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Explain how following design thinking could have avoided this failure.

points.description: Empathise: talking to farmers would reveal their real needs, phones and data limits
Define: the problem would be stated from the farmers' point of view
Prototype: cheap prototypes instead of an expensive full app, so less money is wasted
Test: farmers' feedback would improve the design before launch / iterate

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: By talking to farmers first the company would have learnt what they need and what phones they have. It could then define the real problem, test cheap paper prototypes with farmers, and improve the design from their feedback before spending money on a full app.
